title: Scalable Multiple Electron Transport Architectures for Feedback Traceable Current Sources
authors: Agustin Javier Lapi, Guillermo Fernandez Moroni, Fernando Chierchie, Fabricio Alcalde Bessia, Miqueas Ezequiel Gamero, Brenda Aurea Cervantes Vergara, Blas Junior Irigoyen Gimenez, Eduardo Paolini, Claudio Rodrigo Chavez Blanco, Juan Estrada, Javier Tiffenberg
abstract: We present a scalable electron-counting current cell based on a floating gate architecture operated as a Multiple Electron Transport device (MET). The system enables controlled injection, transport, and precise quantification of discrete charge packets using the sensor non-destructive multiple readout capability. We repurposed the charge-injection technique, jointly with the electron-resolution capability, for a controlled generation of quantized charge packets for an electron-traceable current source.   Scalable architectures based on parallel and series multi-amplifier configurations are explored. Experimental results confirm noise reduction following the square root of the number of independent measurements and demonstrate stable, programmable output current. This approach provides a compact and scalable platform for electron-counting current sources and precision quantum metrology applications.
summary: This paper presents a novel, scalable electron-counting current source based on a floating gate architecture operated as a Multiple Electron Transport device. By using controlled charge injection instead of light, the system achieves absolute charge calibration traceable to the elementary charge. This platform is highly promising for precision quantum metrology applications requiring stable, quantized current sources.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a scalable, highly accurate, and traceable current source capable of precisely counting discrete electron charges.
main_result: The proposed floating gate architecture successfully demonstrates stable, programmable output current with absolute charge calibration traceable to the elementary charge, overcoming limitations of light-based methods.
method: The technique involves controlled charge injection into a Multiple Electron Transport (MET) device (Skipper-CCD) followed by non-destructive, multiple-readout measurement using a MOS amplifier.
model_or_system: The system is an electron-counting current cell built on a floating gate architecture, utilizing parallel and series multi-amplifier configurations for scalability. It operates by generating quantized charge packets via controlled injection rather than illumination.
key_observables: Output current (I), quantized charge packets (up to 2500 e-), and noise reduction quantified by the square root of the number of independent measurements.
important_parameters: Elementary charge (e), noise standard deviation ($\sigma_0$), number of independent measurements ($N_S$), and the dynamic range of calibration (0–2500 e-).
main_assumptions: The closed-loop drain controller block is noted as being outside the scope of the current work; the method overcomes limitations associated with Poisson statistics from optical illumination.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate conceptual sketches of the current cell architectures (basic, general, parallel) and show histograms confirming absolute charge calibration in electrons and time-series plots demonstrating current stability within $3\sigma$ bounds.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for metrologically accurate current sources to detailing the physical platform (MET/Skipper-CCD), describing the charge generation and measurement techniques, analyzing the noise reduction in various scalable architectures (series/parallel), and finally presenting experimental results confirming stability and calibration.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state electronics, the concept of using highly precise, quantized charge detection and feedback control for fundamental physical measurements (like defining the Ampere) touches upon the fundamental limits of measurement in quantum systems.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. (a) is an open-loop Basic current cell conceptual sketch. The open- loop is extended to a closed-loop by adding a charge drain controller block in (b).

Fig. 2. Schematic representation of the proposed architecture. In (a), the current cell is formed by a charge measurement block (CMM), a charge- pump (CP) block, and a memory. The cell is extended in (b), where the CMM can measure the current with different amplifiers, align and average these measurements to obtain a more precise mean current. Many of these CCs can be configured in parallel to achieve an increased current value, as presented in (c).

Fig. 3. Comparison of series and parallel architectures. The simulation parameters correspond to charge packets of 130 k electrons, a single-sample rate of 250 kpix/s, and a measurement time tm of 1 s. (a) Signal as a function of the number of non-destructive measurements (NS) for one-amplifier (blue), ten-series (red), and ten-parallel (magenta) outputs. (b) Noise as a function of NS for the same configurations. The dashed lines indicate the effect of using the quantizer. (c) Relative error (error/current) as a function of current, showing the behavior for increasing NS, NA, and NC in red, blue, and magenta, respectively. For NS and NA, the quantizer response is also shown by dashed lines.

Fig. 4. Left side: Charge injection diagram reflecting the fill and spill technique used to move charge from Vdr of the injection side to H2 in the readout side. The injection is composed of six steps. The two broken lines compress many 3-phase horizontal phases (pixels) conforming the serial register, which separates the injection from the output side. Right side: horizontal charge transfer and readout operation. In states 7 and 8, the charge is moved from the last pixel position H2 to SG, and the charge beneath the sense node is drained. From states 9 to 12, the readout operation of the charge takes place.
Fig. 5. The photograph depicts the Skipper-CCD used to run the experiment, inside a vacuum chamber. The sensor is mounted on a cold plate that keeps it refrigerated at the operating temperature.
